findings.location: exceptions[2] (same defect repeated at quick_review[4], decision_logic[4], timing_deadlines[5]; ma_vs_federal has no entry on this point)
findings.problem: The section presents the federal 60-day LTCF / terminal-illness Schedule II partial-fill window as the operative outer limit and affirmatively instructs the reader not to apply a 30-day deadline to that pathway, without stating the Massachusetts limit that also governs. The section's single ma_vs_federal entry addresses only patient-requested partial fills.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(c) permits LTCF and terminal-illness Schedule II prescriptions to be partially filled and provides that they 'shall be valid for a period not to exceed 60 days from the issue date unless sooner terminated by the discontinuance of medication.' That is a federal ceiling, not a floor. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) provides without qualification that 'a written or electronic prescription for a controlled substance in Schedule II shall become invalid 30 days after the date of issuance,' and s. 18(d3/4) independently requires any remaining portion to be filled not later than 30 days after the issue date. I searched 105 CMR 700.000, 105 CMR 721.000 and 247 CMR 9.00 for an LTCF or terminal-illness carve-out and found none: 105 CMR 700 and 247 CMR 9 contain no LTCF, terminal-illness or partial-fill provision at all, and 105 CMR 721.055 restates the 30-day remaining-portion limit with no exception. In Massachusetts the prescription is therefore dead on day 31, and a pharmacist who follows exceptions[2] and dispenses a further partial quantity on, say, day 45 to an LTCF resident dispenses a Schedule II drug on an invalid prescription. This is the single most consequential defect in the batch because the section tells the reader to disregard a 30-day limit that in fact controls.

findings.problem: The decision tree routes an LTCF resident or terminally ill patient to 'partial fillings may continue for no more than 60 days from issue' as the action, with no Massachusetts condition attached, so the tree returns an unlawful answer for Massachusetts facts on days 31 through 60.
findings.rationale: The section's stated method (learning_objectives[1]) is to choose the correct deadline by identifying the pathway. Applied to the LTCF branch in Massachusetts the method yields 60 days, but M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) has already invalidated the written or electronic Schedule II prescription at 30 days. Every other branch of this tree pairs the federal rule with the Massachusetts condition that also reaches the facts (see decision_logic[2] and decision_logic[6]); the LTCF branch is the one place where the pairing is missing, and it is the branch where the two sources diverge most.

findings.problem: The deadline table records 'LTCF or terminal-illness Schedule II partial fills - Up to 60 days from issue unless discontinued sooner' as an operative deadline in a Massachusetts study guide, with the consequence stated as 'further partial dispensing must stop at the 60-day limit or upon earlier discontinuation.'
findings.rationale: A candidate memorising this table will carry '60 days' into a Massachusetts question. The controlling Massachusetts deadline is 30 days from issuance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a), and the correct consequence is that further partial dispensing must stop at 30 days from issue, at the 60-day federal ceiling, or upon earlier discontinuation, whichever comes first. The table entry as written is the number a candidate would select and it is the wrong number for Massachusetts.

findings.problem: The only statement about LTCF and terminal-illness documentation is that such partial fills 'must use the special federal documentation framework for that pathway.' The entry raises the duty and then conveys none of its content.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(c) requires the pharmacist to record on the prescription whether the patient is 'terminally ill' or an 'LTCF patient,' and provides that 'a prescription that is partially filled and does not contain the notation "terminally ill" or "LTCF patient" shall be deemed to have been filled in violation of the Act.' It further requires, for each partial filling, a record of the date, quantity dispensed, remaining quantity authorized, and the identity of the dispensing pharmacist, and requires the pharmacist to contact the practitioner if terminal-illness classification is in doubt. The missing notation is not a paperwork detail; its absence converts an otherwise lawful partial fill into a violation. A content-free pointer leaves a candidate unable to identify the one act that makes the fill lawful.

findings.location: forms_records[0] (and the absence of any federal partial-fill notation entry in forms_records)
findings.problem: forms_records states the Massachusetts patient-record notation duty for partial fills but the section nowhere states the parallel federal notation duties, leaving the impression that partial-fill notation is a Massachusetts-only requirement.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(a) conditions the stock-shortage partial fill itself on the pharmacist making 'a notation of the quantity supplied on the face of the written prescription, written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic prescription record.' 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(5)(ii) requires, for a patient-requested partial fill, a notation reading 'The [patient, parent or legal guardian of a minor patient, or caregiver of an adult patient named in a medical power of attorney] requested partial fill on [date]' plus the quantity dispensed, and a dispensing record carrying the information required by 21 CFR 1306.22(c). Because this section is the guide's home for Schedule II partial fills and carries a ma_vs_federal field, presenting only the Massachusetts notation invites the inference that a pharmacist outside the Massachusetts patient-record duty has no notation obligation. The federal notation is a precondition of the lawful partial fill under 1306.13(a).

findings.location: forms_records (no entry for emergency oral Schedule II records; compare quick_review[1]-[3] and timing_deadlines[0])
findings.problem: The section covers the emergency oral Schedule II quantity limit and the seven-day follow-up but never states the record requirements that sit in the same provision.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(2) requires the pharmacist to reduce the oral prescription to writing immediately with all information required by 21 CFR 1306.05 except the practitioner's signature. 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) requires the follow-up prescription to have 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' and the date of the oral order written on its face, requires the pharmacist to attach the paper follow-up to the oral order reduced to writing, and requires annotation of the electronic prescription record where the follow-up is electronic. Learning objective 3 declares the emergency oral follow-up requirements to be in scope, so a candidate should be able to say what a compliant follow-up looks like and cannot from this section.

findings.problem: The section states the pharmacist's duty to notify the DEA when the emergency oral follow-up does not arrive, but omits the consequence the regulation attaches to not notifying.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) provides that 'failure of the pharmacist to do so shall void the authority conferred by this paragraph to dispense without a written prescription of a prescribing individual practitioner.' The notification is therefore the condition on which the pharmacist's own earlier emergency dispensing remains lawful, not merely a report about the prescriber's default. A candidate who reads the duty as a courtesy report will underrate it, and the sanction falls on the pharmacist rather than the prescriber.

results.summary: Most of this section is sound and I confirmed the hard points against the primary text. 21 CFR 1306.12(a) does flatly prohibit refilling a Schedule II prescription, and the section's refill-versus-remainder distinction is correct. The three partial-fill pathways are separated correctly and each carries the right number: 1306.13(a) ties the 72-hour remainder to the pharmacy's inability to supply the full quantity and requires prescriber notification and a new prescription thereafter; 1306.13(b)(2) sets the request-based remainder at not later than 30 days after the date the prescription was written; and that same paragraph carries the emergency-oral exception fixing the remainder at not later than 72 hours after issue, which the section correctly isolates at exceptions[1] and timing_deadlines[4]. The emergency oral rules are correctly split: 1306.11(d)(1) limits the quantity to the amount adequate to treat the patient during the emergency period, (d)(3) imposes the reasonable-effort identification duty only where the practitioner is not known to the pharmacist, (d)(4) puts the seven-day delivery duty on the prescriber and the DEA-notification duty on the pharmacist. On the Massachusetts side I confirmed every claim: s. 23(a) invalidates a written or electronic Schedule II prescription 30 days after issuance; s. 18(d3/4) makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory ('shall, if requested by the patient'), confines the remaining portion to the same pharmacy, requires the patient-record notation accessible to the prescriber on request, and sets 30 days from issue for the remaining portion; and the five-day limit in that subsection genuinely reaches only prescriptions filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), which exceptions[3] states accurately. s. 22(c) does require the opioid Schedule II partial-fill notation on the prescription, in an amount not to exceed the full prescribed quantity, as forms_records[2] says. The defect that blocks release is the LTCF and terminal-illness branch. The section states the federal 60-day window four times, once as an affirmative instruction not to apply a 30-day deadline to that pathway, and never pairs it with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a), which invalidates the prescription at 30 days with no LTCF or terminal-illness exception anywhere in c. 94C, 105 CMR 700.000, 105 CMR 721.000 or 247 CMR 9.00. A Massachusetts candidate following the section would dispense on an invalid Schedule II prescription. Secondary defects: forms_records reduces the 1306.13(c) documentation framework to a content-free pointer even though a partial fill lacking the 'terminally ill' or 'LTCF patient' notation is deemed filled in violation of the Act; the federal partial-fill notations under 1306.13(a) and (b)(5) are absent while the Massachusetts one is present; and the emergency-oral record formalities and the voiding consequence of a missed DEA notification are omitted. Two minor imprecisions I did not treat as findings: decision_logic[2] and [3] describe the requester as 'the patient or prescriber' where 1306.13(b)(1)(iii) also reaches a parent or legal guardian of a minor and a caregiver named in an adult patient's medical power of attorney; and the section does not state 1306.13(b)(1)(iv)'s cap that all partial fillings together may not exceed the total quantity prescribed, which is however conveyed indirectly through the s. 22(c) notation at forms_records[2]. Practice mapping is sound: MA-Q-0011, MA-Q-0012, MA-Q-0021, MA-Q-0094, MA-Q-0104 and MA-Q-0401 are all RELEASED and each turns on a proposition the section teaches (completed Schedule II cannot be refilled; 30-day Massachusetts validity; request-based 30-day remainder; stock-shortage 72-hour remainder; DEA notification after a missed follow-up; the five-day limit reaching only the out-of-state pathways).

findings.problem: The section presents 21 CFR 1306.25 refill-purpose transfer as the whole federal transfer framework and never mentions the separate federal rule governing transfer of an electronic controlled-substance prescription for initial dispensing.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.08(e) provides that 'the transfer for initial dispensing of an electronic prescription for a controlled substance in Schedule II-V is permissible between retail pharmacies, upon request from the patient, on a one-time basis only,' and that where the prescription is Schedule III, IV or V with authorised refills the refills travel with it. 1306.08(f) and (g) add the mechanics and the state-law condition. Two consequences matter for a Massachusetts candidate. First, an unfilled electronic Schedule II prescription is transferable once on patient request, which a reader of this section would deny outright. Second, the real-time shared-database exception in 1306.25(a) that the section teaches at exceptions[2] has no counterpart in 1306.08, so importing it into an initial-dispensing transfer would exceed the federal permission. The gap is inside the section's declared scope: its title is 'Schedule III-V Refills and Massachusetts Transfers,' learning objective 2 is to 'separate transfer eligibility from the prescription's remaining lawful refill capacity,' and 247 CMR 9.14(1) imposes a schedule-neutral duty to transfer at the patient's request in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy.

findings.problem: The section assigns transfer duties only to entities ('receiving pharmacy', 'transferring pharmacy') and never says which individuals may execute a transfer, although a linked practice question turns on exactly that.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.25(b)(1) requires that a Schedule III-V refill transfer 'must be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists,' and 21 CFR 1306.08(f)(3) imposes the same requirement on an initial-dispensing electronic transfer. Massachusetts draws the complementary line: 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) permits a certified pharmacy technician, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, to perform prescription transfers between pharmacies 'for prescriptions issued for controlled substances in Schedule VI only.' Together these settle who may transfer what, and the section teaches neither half. MA-Q-0120, which this section links, requires the candidate to affirm that a certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI transfer with pharmacist approval; nothing in the section supports that answer, and because the item is select-all, missing it loses the question.

findings.problem: The Massachusetts Schedule V six-month limit is rendered as a bar on refilling only. The consequence field reads 'no refill after the state time limit or after five refills,' which leaves an initial fill of an old Schedule V prescription apparently permitted.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.04(13) reads: 'A licensee may not fill or refill a prescription for a Schedule V controlled substance more than six months after the date on which said prescription was issued. A prescription for a Schedule V controlled substance may not be refilled more than five times.' The six-month limit reaches the first dispensing as well as refills, exactly as 21 CFR 1306.22(a) does for Schedules III and IV. The section gets this right for the federal rule at timing_deadlines[0] ('no further fill or refill after the federal time limit') and wrong for the Massachusetts rule in the very next entry. A candidate presented with a never-dispensed Schedule V prescription seven months old would read this section as permitting the initial fill; 9.04(13) forbids it.

results.summary: The legal statements in this section are accurate and several of the fine points are unusually well drawn. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) does bar filling or refilling a Schedule III or IV prescription more than six months after issue and bars more than five refills, and timing_deadlines[0] correctly states the consequence as reaching fills as well as refills. 21 CFR 1306.25(a) does permit a refill-purpose Schedule III-V transfer 'on a one-time basis only' with the real-time shared-database exception, and 1306.25(b)(2) does impose the VOID annotation and transferee record on the transferring pharmacist; quick_review[3], exceptions[2] and the second half of role_duties[1] track the text. 247 CMR 9.14(1)-(3) does require a timely transfer at the request of the patient or agent so as not to delay therapy, does permit the pharmacy to act as the patient's agent, and does forbid a transfer fee; 9.14(4)(a)-(c) does put Schedule VI transfers on the Schedule III-V footing, does allow the remaining authorised refills to move, and does bar transfer of a refill-authorising Schedule VI prescription more than one year from issuance. I confirmed 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 9.04(13), so the facility-scope caveat at exceptions[1] and decision_logic[2] is real and correctly identified. The oral follow-up material is the strongest part of the section and I verified all of it. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) requires an electronic follow-up within 2 days, or a written follow-up within not more than 7 days where the practitioner holds a s. 23(h) exception, postmarked within that period, and expressly does not apply to Schedule VI. 105 CMR 721.070(B) independently sets 'not more than seven business days' for an oral Schedule II-V prescription issued under a 721.070(A) exception. exceptions[3] and common_traps[4] flag that divergence accurately rather than papering over it. The out-of-state oral Schedule III-V duty in s. 18(c) really is a duty on the pharmacist to record that he has requested the writing, with the seven-day period running on the practitioner's delivery or mailing, which common_traps[2] states correctly. Three gaps stop this short of release. The federal initial-dispensing electronic transfer rule in 21 CFR 1306.08(e)-(g), which reaches Schedules II through V and has no shared-database exception, is absent from a section whose declared job is to separate transfer eligibility from remaining refill capacity. Nothing tells the candidate who may execute a transfer, although 1306.25(b)(1) demands two licensed pharmacists and 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) confines certified-technician transfers to Schedule VI, and linked question MA-Q-0120 tests the technician point. And 247 CMR 9.04(13) is rendered as a refill-only bar when it also forbids the initial fill after six months. Two smaller wording points I did not treat as findings: quick_review[0]'s 'unless renewed by the practitioner' is loose, since 21 CFR 1306.22(e)(5) caps an oral refill authorisation at five refills and six months from the original issue date and the limits can only be escaped by a new prescription; and quick_review[4] states the oral follow-up duty for 'a Massachusetts oral controlled-substance prescription' without the Schedule VI carve-out, which timing_deadlines[4] then supplies. Practice mapping passes. MA-Q-0009, MA-Q-0120 and MA-Q-0397 are all RELEASED. MA-Q-0397 maps cleanly onto 247 CMR 9.14(2) and (3). MA-Q-0120 maps onto 9.14(1) and (4) apart from the technician option noted above. MA-Q-0009 is a weaker fit: only its option E, rejecting import of the federal Schedule III-IV refill rule into a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug, is a proposition this section teaches, while its other four options turn on pregabalin and gabapentin scheduling, MassPAT reporting and CMEA retail controls that this section does not cover. That is a study-design limitation rather than a legal-fidelity defect, so I passed the criterion, but a candidate cannot answer MA-Q-0009 from this section alone.

findings.location: decision_logic[2] and role_duties (no entry naming who may perform a Schedule VI transfer)
findings.problem: The section teaches the Schedule VI transfer pathway and the one-year transfer limit but never states who may carry out the transfer, even though the Schedule VI-only technician authority is the distinctive Massachusetts scope-of-practice consequence of the Schedule VI classification and a linked question tests it.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) provides that 'a certified pharmacy technician may, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, perform prescription transfers between pharmacies for prescriptions issued for controlled substances in Schedule VI only.' The 'only' is the point: for federally scheduled prescriptions 21 CFR 1306.25(b)(1) and 1306.08(f)(3) require the transfer to be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, so Schedule VI is the single schedule where a technician may do the work. The section's learning objective 2 puts Massachusetts transfer rules in scope, the authority sits inside the section's own MA-RX-TRANSFER dependency, and linked question MA-Q-0120 requires the candidate to affirm the technician's authority as one of three correct options in a select-all item. A candidate studying only this section would either omit that option or, worse, generalise a technician transfer to a Schedule III-V prescription.

results.summary: This section is accurate on every point I checked against the primary text, and it draws two distinctions that are easy to get wrong. 105 CMR 700.002(F) does define Schedule VI as 'all prescription drugs, which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner,' so quick_review[0] and ma_vs_federal[0] are right that Schedule VI is a Massachusetts classification carrying no federal scheduling consequence. 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9) does except Schedule VI prescriptions from the electronic-prescribing requirement, and the opening words of 721.070(A) preserve every other prescription requirement, so quick_review[1], exceptions[0] and common_traps[0] are correct that the exception removes the format mandate and nothing else; 721.070(C) confirms role_duties[0]'s framing by relieving the receiving pharmacist of any duty to verify that an exception applies. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) does require immediate reduction of an oral prescription to writing with the listed information, and the last sentence of s. 20(c) does exclude Schedule VI from the later follow-up-document duty only, which quick_review[2] and forms_records[0] state precisely. 247 CMR 9.04(12) does make a Schedule VI prescription valid for one year from the date of issue, does bar a licensee from refilling it after one year, and does permit a professional-judgment continuation not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging where the prescription has expired or has no refills left and prescriber authorisation cannot be obtained in a timely manner. 247 CMR 9.04(15) does exclude institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 9.04(12), so exceptions[2] is exact. common_traps[2] is the sharpest item in the batch: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c)'s one-year bar on transferring a refill-authorising Schedule VI prescription and 247 CMR 9.04(12)'s one-year validity really are two different rules that happen to share a number, and the section refuses to conflate them. 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8) does let the Commissioner designate an additional drug on a bona fide potential for abuse, on the four listed factors, and does require notice to all dispensers that they must begin reporting; 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) and (A)(3) and 247 CMR 9.04(14)(b) do extend PMP reporting and the customer identifier to an additional drug, and 9.04(14)(c) does carry the documented serious-hardship route with the recipient's printed name, address and signature. quick_review[4], forms_records[1] and common_traps[3] track all of that. The one gap is scope of practice on transfers: the section never says that 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) lets a certified pharmacy technician perform transfers for Schedule VI only, with pharmacist-on-duty approval, which is both the distinctive Schedule VI consequence and a required answer in the linked MA-Q-0120. One cross-cutting observation I did not treat as a finding against this section: 247 CMR 9.04(10) directs that in determining whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after the prescription was written as day one. That convention governs the Schedule VI one-year clock this section teaches, but it equally governs every validity clock in this batch and no section states it, so it reads as a guide-level omission rather than a defect in this section's declared scope. Practice mapping passes. MA-Q-0116, MA-Q-0118 and MA-Q-0120 are all RELEASED. MA-Q-0116 turns on the s. 20(c) Schedule VI carve-out against the surviving s. 20(a) duty, which quick_review[2] teaches directly. MA-Q-0118 turns on required prescription elements surviving Schedule VI status, which exceptions[0] and role_duties[0] teach. MA-Q-0120 turns on 247 CMR 9.14, taught here, plus the technician point noted above.

I checked every substantive proposition in this section against the primary text and found no defect. quick_review[0] is precisely right on the point candidates most often invert: 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1)(i) conditions the patient-requested Schedule II partial fill on the fill not being 'prohibited by State law,' not on State law affirmatively authorising it, and quick_review[0]'s 'alongside the other federal conditions in 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1)' correctly keeps the remaining conditions in view. common_traps[2] states the same point in the direction that matters for a silent jurisdiction. The Massachusetts overlay is complete against M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4). Every condition that subsection imposes appears somewhere in the section: the mandatory lesser-quantity dispensing on patient request at ma_vs_federal[0], the same-pharmacy restriction and patient-record notation at quick_review[1] and forms_records[0], the 30-day remaining-portion limit at timing_deadlines[0], and the five-day initial-dispensing limit correctly confined to the s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) out-of-state pathways at timing_deadlines[3] and exceptions[2]. I cross-checked that confinement against 105 CMR 721.055(A), which operationalises the same limit by the prescriber's out-of-Commonwealth address, and against 721.055(B) and (C), which restate the same-pharmacy rule, the 30-day limit and the notation duty; nothing in the regulation broadens the five-day limit to an in-state prescription. exceptions[2] correctly identifies the emergency-oral displacement: under 1306.13(b)(2) the remaining portion of a partially filled emergency oral Schedule II prescription must be filled not later than 72 hours after issue rather than within the ordinary 30 days. The refill-limit comparison is accurate on both sides and correctly scoped. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) supplies the five-refill and six-month limits for Schedules III and IV; 247 CMR 9.04(13) supplies numerically identical limits for Schedule V as a matter of Massachusetts law; and 247 CMR 9.04(15) does exclude institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 9.04(13), so quick_review[2], ma_vs_federal[1] and exceptions[1] are each verified. common_traps[1] correctly warns against transplanting a right number from the wrong schedule. forms_records[1] tracks M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) faithfully, including its 'not to exceed the full prescribed quantity' formulation. I noted that 105 CMR 721.020(D)(7) phrases the same notation as an amount 'less than the recommended full quantity indicated'; the section cites and follows the statute, which is the correct choice, and the divergence does not change any answer. Two things I looked for and considered before passing the section. First, the section confines itself to the patient-requested partial-fill and refill-limit interactions and does not reach the federal 60-day LTCF and terminal-illness window, which collides with the 30-day Massachusetts Schedule II validity in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a); that pathway is outside this section's declared rule set and its methodological objectives, so I treated the omission as a scope choice rather than a defect. It is worth recording that this section's own method, applied to that pathway, is what exposes the defect I found in SG-CII-LIFECYCLE. Second, timing_deadlines[1] labels its event as a refill, whereas both 1306.22(a) and 247 CMR 9.04(13) bar the initial fill after six months as well; the entry is thin rather than wrong, the six-month limit is stated as an issue-date limit at quick_review[2], and the refill window is owned by SG-CIII-V-REFILL-TRANSFER, so I did not treat it as a finding here. Practice mapping passes. MA-Q-0009, MA-Q-0021 and MA-Q-0401 are all RELEASED. MA-Q-0021 turns on choosing the request-based 30-day window over the 72-hour shortage rule, taught at quick_review[0] and timing_deadlines[0]. MA-Q-0401 turns on the five-day limit reaching only the out-of-state pathways, taught at timing_deadlines[3] and exceptions[2]. MA-Q-0009's option E is a direct test of common_traps[1] and ma_vs_federal[1]; its remaining options draw on drug-classification, MassPAT and CMEA material outside this section, so the item exercises the section's proposition but is not answerable from the section alone.
